Reporting issue 0, key finding 4 note, analysis.effect_sizes and results_show: the Table 1 recalculation (−0.29, I² 89%) holds only when the Dawe 2011 and Hajebi 2018 dispersions are read as standard errors; taken as printed, −0.35 (−0.90 to 0.20), I² 94%; neither reproduces Fig. 1.

Exposure and outcome windows corrected in design_detail, can_establish, cannot_establish, abstinence_at_testing, key finding 2, results_show, claimed and the RoB domain note: use since the previous interview, symptoms over the past month at ages 18–25.

design_detail, can_establish, key finding 2 and claimed: the fixed confounders include adolescent factors (p. 2; Results point 1, p. 4), not only childhood and family factors (adjudicator's consistency fix, following AI reader 15's note on the claim).
for_senior_author: Interpretation gap: AI reader 15 would rate it substantial rather than minor (the abstract's 2.85 next to the fully adjusted estimates; 'no persistent vulnerability' resting on an imprecise comparison; 'an independent risk factor for psychosis' from self-reported symptom items reported at the same interviews). for_senior_author: Post-exposure interventions domain: AI reader 16 proposes low (interventions probably uncommon in a general-population cohort, no mechanism by exposure); the card keeps some concerns. Overall high unchanged either way.

Key finding 4, its page, locator and note, and analysis.effect_sizes: the oral-fluid result is averaged over weeks 4, 8 and 12, not a week-12 value; 86.8% and 88.0% of samples were not methamphetamine-negative.

Reporting issue 6: the any-adverse-event total, 300 of 339, is 88.5%, printed 89.

for_senior_author: The overall rating changed from low to critically low only because item 4 was applied as written, as this brief directs; the readers agree on every other item, so the card is ai-checked. If the senior author chooses the lenient reading of item 4 for the project, this card returns to low confidence (provisional).

amstar2_item4.rule_applied: AMSTAR 2 item 4 gives partial yes only if at least two databases were searched, keywords or a strategy are given, and publication restrictions such as language are justified (Shea et al., 2017). An unjustified language limit therefore gives no; the overall confidence was recomputed from the critical domains.

this_batch.overall: critically-low (unchanged; no longer depends on item 7)

earlier_cards_applied_the_other_way.reason: English-language only without justification, stated in its own item 4 note.

earlier_cards_to_check.reason: Language limits are not described in the main text and the search strings are in a supplement that was not read; if the supplement shows an unjustified language limit, item 4 becomes no.

decisions.wording: Corrected: the network estimates against risperidone are differences in end-of-treatment scores (the review used final values for all symptom analyses, p. 7), not in how much symptoms fell; statement and magnitude reworded. Every number checked against the PDF. Plain text unchanged (says no more than the statement).
decisions.status: replicated → single-study. The claim rests on one network meta-analysis whose six trial reports are unread; the trials test five different drug pairs and the review reports only that each found no significant difference, not each trial's direction, so the METHODS §6.4 condition for counting pooled trials is not met, and a run of non-significant head-to-head results is not a replicated finding (AI reader 15's view).
decisions.grade: Very low unchanged (start high; risk of bias −1, indirectness −1, imprecision −2). Reasoning adds that inconsistency can hardly be judged: the global I² of 0% rests on one degree of freedom from the two aripiprazole–risperidone trials.
decisions.verification: Not narrative-only (Srisurapanont et al., 2021, is a systematic review and network meta-analysis read in full); every anchor ai-checked, so the claim stays ai-anchored, above metadata-verified.

questions.replicated or single study: Single study, for the reasons above; reader 12's 'six trials in the same direction' counts non-significant results of different comparisons as one replicated finding.

for_senior_author: When the 24-month trial of aripiprazole or paliperidone against treatment as usual (Chung et al., 2026) is read, the status and the claim's open question (benefit beyond usual care or abstinence) should be revisited.

decisions.wording: Statement adds that only about a third of the Japanese studies (35%, against 6% elsewhere) used ICD-10, so the review's diagnostic explanation is partial (Voce et al., 2019, p. 6). Plain text unchanged.
decisions.status: mixed kept: persistence beyond a month ranges from 0% to 96% with wide unexplained spread within the review's own subgroups (18–96% in Japan, 0–39% elsewhere), and later schizophrenia diagnoses run from 5% to about 39%; the inconsistency is in size, not in whether persistence occurs.
decisions.grade: Very low unchanged (start low; risk of bias −1, inconsistency −1). Two reasons corrected: the laboratory studies observed no persistence (not impossible by design), and the Japanese studies did not mostly use ICD-10.
decisions.verification: Not narrative-only (Voce et al., 2019, systematic review read in full); all anchors ai-checked; stays ai-anchored.

decisions.wording: Statement says the negative-symptom difference is consistent in direction (10 of 12 study estimates, none significantly the other way; significant in 5 studies from four research groups). Positive symptoms described as reported (−0.01, −0.13 to 0.11, I² 0%), with the statement that none of the 12 study values can be reproduced from the review's Table 1 and both recalculations given (−0.29, −0.67 to 0.10, I² 89%, reading two studies' dispersions as standard errors, as the review's own negative-symptom values require; −0.35, −0.90 to 0.20, I² 94%, as printed), concluding no significant difference rather than similarity. Magnitude: the reported leave-one-out (−0.254) does not name the study left out; recalculations added. Plain text unchanged.
decisions.status: mixed kept, as one claim: the positive-symptom comparison is inconsistent on recalculation (study values significant in both directions), while the negative-symptom difference is consistent; the statement now says which part is consistent.
decisions.grade: Very low unchanged (start low; risk of bias −1, inconsistency −1). Inconsistency reason restated; the narrative review's table–text disagreement moved out of inconsistency (a reporting problem).
decisions.verification: Not narrative-only (Cohen-Laroque et al., 2024, read in full); all anchors ai-checked; stays ai-anchored.

questions.one claim or two: One claim. Both comparisons come from the same review, the same 12 studies and the same biases (treated cross-sectional groups, mixed acute and persistent psychosis, probable double counting), and readers need them together to see that the conditions overlap; splitting is not clearly needed once the statement says that the negative-symptom difference is consistent and the positive-symptom comparison is not.
questions.Cohen-Laroque positive-symptom pooled re: Report it as the review's result, say that its study-level values cannot be reproduced from the review's own Table 1 (the fault lies in the inputs, since the Fig. 1 values pool to the reported result), give both recalculations with their assumption, and never cite it as evidence that positive symptoms are similar.

for_senior_author: If the at-a-glance display shows only the status label, a split into a negative-symptom claim (replicated, very low: low minus one for risk of bias) and a positive-symptom claim (mixed, very low) would label each part exactly; recommended only in that case.

decisions.wording: Corrected against Boden et al. (2023, p. 2): at ages 18–25 symptoms were asked for the past month and use for the period since the previous interview, so use and symptoms were reported at the same interviews, not for the same periods; the fixed confounders include adolescent factors, and the 2.85 is not adjusted for concurrent cannabis use. Plain text aligned with the statement (self-reported psychotic experiences; ever at least weekly use), as AI reader 15 proposed.
decisions.status: replicated kept: the four adjusted studies come from different groups and countries and the New Zealand birth cohort is an independent sample, all agreeing in direction; the shared author (McKetin) does not make it the same team.
decisions.grade: Low unchanged (start low, no downgrade, no upgrade). Reasoning adds that Boden's frequency categories are not monotonic (1.37, 1.32, 2.85) and that the top category has 51 people.
decisions.verification: Not narrative-only; all anchors ai-checked; stays ai-anchored.

for_senior_author: The Boden card's interpretation gap (minor on the card, substantial in AI reader 15's view) bears on how strongly the claim should present the cohort; see the card entry.

decisions.wording: Plain text: three overstatements removed (AI reader 16's version): 'severe' poisoning, a frequency attached to the other signs, and an unhedged statement that many deaths come from accidents, suicide and homicide. Statement and magnitude note that the review's Table 1 gives the chest-pain study 171 patients against 36 in the text.
decisions.status: mixed → replicated. What the claim asserts, sympathomimetic and psychiatric features whose frequency varies several-fold, is reported consistently by independent series in several countries (tachycardia and hypertension in Perth and Taipei; psychosis or paranoia in Perth, Oregon, Seattle and Honolulu), and none reports their absence; the variation in frequency is part of the statement and is rated under GRADE inconsistency, not in the label. Shared and linked series counted once.
decisions.grade: Very low unchanged (start low; risk of bias −1, inconsistency −1 for the frequencies, indirectness −1).
decisions.verification: Not narrative-only (Sibanda et al., 2019, is a systematic review with a reported search, read in full); all anchors ai-checked; stays ai-anchored.

for_senior_author: The systematic review pooled nothing on this claim's outcome, so every figure remains second-hand (as the statement says); the narrative-review rule (METHODS §6.3) does not apply by its letter, though part of its rationale does (AI reader 16's note).

decisions.wording: Plain text: the Australian 45.7% is lifetime (had ever met the criteria by the interview), not current, and the criteria were asked only of people who had used at least five times (AI reader 16's wording). Statement unchanged (checked against both PDFs).
decisions.status: mixed → single-study. The claim itself holds that the two surveys measure different quantities and rates no inconsistency, so 'mixed' (inconsistent findings on a common quantity) does not apply; each figure rests on one survey and neither replicates the other.
decisions.grade: Very low unchanged (start low; risk of bias −1 for the Australian figures, indirectness −2). Reasoning adds why imprecision is not rated (the 50.4% has no interval).
decisions.verification: Not narrative-only; all anchors ai-checked; stays ai-anchored.

for_senior_author: Splitting into a US claim and an Australian claim, each single-study, would make the label literally true for each; recommended if a claim citing two surveys under 'single study' is judged confusing.

decisions.wording: Statement and magnitude: the weekly-use analysis is adjusted for childhood and adolescent factors only and is not period-matched (heaviest use in any period against violence at any time from 18 to 35; Foulds et al., 2020, 2.7, p. 3). Plain text: the behaviour-versus-offending contrast is unadjusted, and the weekly-use result took fewer factors into account (AI reader 16's wording).
decisions.status: mixed kept: in the review's unadjusted data violent behaviour and violent offending point different ways (3.7 against 1.0, I² 94% unexplained within offending), while the adjusted estimates agree in direction; the reasoning now says so, since inconsistency is not rated down.
decisions.grade: Very low unchanged (start low; risk of bias −1, imprecision −1; no dose–response upgrade). One reason corrected: the cohort's fully adjusted intervals exclude 1 for perpetration and intimate-partner perpetration, so 'neither source can exclude no association' was wrong; the reasoning now says the lower limits sit at 1.00–1.04 in one cohort at high risk of bias.
decisions.verification: Not narrative-only; all anchors ai-checked; stays ai-anchored. The changelog of 0.5.0 calls the quotation 11 words; it has 12 (within the limit), noted in the new entry.

decisions.wording: Statement: no count or share of opioid co-involvement is printed (Figure 1A plots rates; the two opioid series overlap). Plain text: the latest year is provisional. Reasoning: the 2021–2023 segment rests on three yearly values, the last provisional.
decisions.status: single-study kept: Zhu et al. (2025) and Han et al. (2021) count the same national death records (overlapping 2015–2019), so the later analysis extends the series rather than replicating it; the survey figures come from Han et al. alone.
decisions.grade: Low unchanged (descriptive, start low, never upgraded; Zhu's faults affect exact figures, not the direction or the timing of the slowdown).
decisions.verification: Not narrative-only; all anchors ai-checked; stays ai-anchored.

for_senior_author: AI reader 16 suggests that METHODS §6.4 say explicitly that re-analyses of one registry count as one source (here they are labelled single study, not replicated by the same team).

decisions.wording: Corrected against McKetin et al. (2026, pp. 583–585): the 2.2 days is a larger fall from baseline (7.0 against 4.8 days), not fewer days at week 12, where the arms differed by about 1.1 days because the mirtazapine arm started about 1 day higher (editors' calculation); the oral-fluid result is averaged over weeks 4, 8 and 12; the excess stopping for medication-related reasons (23% vs 15%) is not clearly beyond chance (printed P = .19; about .05 on recalculation). Plain text replaced by AI reader 17's version ('cutting down their use by about 2 more days in 4 weeks'; 'a difference that could be due to chance').
decisions.status: replicated kept, now resting on the Coffin et al. (2020)–McKetin et al. (2026) pair, which shares no author (reference records), site, sample or analysis model and agrees in direction on primary outcomes. Colfax–McKetin share Steven Shoptaw and Colfax–Coffin are the same team, so neither of those pairs counts.
decisions.grade: Low unchanged (start high; risk of bias −1, inconsistency −1). Risk-of-bias reason adds the Australian trial's 14% missing week-12 data under missing-at-random assumptions; imprecision gives the strict reading: against a minimal important difference rather than the null it could be rated down, giving very low.
decisions.verification: Not narrative-only; all anchors ai-checked; stays ai-anchored.

questions.replicated or replicated by the same tea: Replicated (Coffin 2020 and McKetin 2026 share no authors; the one shared investigator links McKetin only with Colfax 2011, which is same-team with Coffin anyway).
questions.plain text '2 fewer days': Changed: it read as a difference in use at the end of treatment; the plain text now says people on mirtazapine reported cutting down their use by about 2 more days in 4 weeks.

for_senior_author: Strict reading of imprecision: if the senior author rates imprecision against a minimal important difference (none is stated by the trials), the claim becomes very low.

Disclosure: Coffin (first author of the second San Francisco trial) and Shoptaw are both authors of a bupropion trial (Trivedi et al., 2021), a link outside the mirtazapine trials that the §6.4 rule does not count.

Outside the claim file: data/site/simple.json still carries the pre-update short answer for this question (AI reader 17); it needs rewriting from the patched claim (WRITING-RULES), which this adjudication may not edit.

AI reader 17 expected a validator warning for the causal relation 'reduces' at low certainty; validate.py warns only for evidence that starts low, so there is none here (randomized trials). The statement's own verb ('was followed by') fits the rating; no change made.

decisions.wording: Statement, magnitude and plain text: the later bupropion meta-analysis does not state its unit of analysis; that samples were the unit is the editors' reading of its tables ('appears to have counted every test as if it came from a different person'); its urine reports all share investigators with one another; its retention pool appears to omit one stage of the combination trial.
decisions.status: replicated kept: it rests on the abstinence pooling of five trials from two investigator groups (OR 0.97, I² 2%), which share no author in the lists available although both have authors on a third trial outside the pool (Elkashef et al., 2008); Bakouni et al. (2023) enters only as qualifying evidence on a different outcome.
decisions.grade: Very low unchanged (start high; risk of bias −1, imprecision −2).
decisions.verification: Not narrative-only; all anchors ai-checked; stays ai-anchored.
